Welcome to The Moral Imperative, the second session of the Digital Conversion: Every Child, Every Day course. This session should take you approximately 75 minutes to complete.

You’ll need your Participant Workbook and your copy of Every Child, Every Day: A Digital Conversion Model for Student Achievement. Go ahead and pause the video while you get these resources. Click Play when you are ready to continue.

Before you begin, review what you learned in Session 1.

You learned about the organization of the Common Core State Standards for Mathematics-or the CCSSM. You explored how the CCSSM are integrated into Investigations for the Common Core.

You learned how to use your Core Curriculum Package to fully align your mathematics instruction to the CCSSM.

Finally, you focused deeply on the Standards for Mathematical Practice and learned how these standards are embedded in the fabric of Investigations.

Now, let’s look at the Session 2 objectives.

By the end of this session, you will be able to

·define moral imperative; and
·explain the relationship between high expectations and the moral imperative for digital conversion.

Before you begin the session, you’ll review content that you learned in Session 1 by watching a short video. Click the video to hear Dr. Scott Smith, the Chief Technology Officer in Mooresville Graded School District, discuss the rationale for the digital conversion and how the district introduced technology into the schools.

Let’s look at a definition for moral imperative provided by Macmillan Publishers Limited. Moral imperative is “something that must happen because it is the right thing.”

Take a few minutes to reflect on your role in the classroom, school, or district. Think about your moral imperative for becoming involved in your school or district. Then, complete the following statement in your Participant Workbook: My moral imperative for becoming involved in this school or district is . . .

For example, as a teacher, your moral imperative may be to help students learn and let students know you care about them. If you are a curriculum supervisor, you may feel the need to help teachers learn in order to increase student learning in their classrooms. As a principal, you may feel that you have a moral obligation to help students learn so they have better life opportunities. Finally, as a superintendent, you may want to increase student learning by supporting teachers and school administrators.

When you are ready, click Next to continue.

According to Douglas B. Reeves, author and founder of The Leadership and Learning Center, “‛ children can learn’ does not mean ‘all children are the same.’ Furthermore, diversity is not merely about external characteristics. If we are really going to take this seriously, that means we start looking at diversity on the inside as well as the outside. Making this principle both a moral and intellectual part of the curriculum will require . . . a diversity of approaches, diversity of techniques, and a diversity of teaching strategies.”

Think about your answer to the question about moral imperative. It is likely that you included reasons such as helping students learn or caring for students in a way that will help increase their opportunities in life. The moral imperative behind teaching, learning, and making changes in teaching strategies is the same moral imperative behind digital conversion-namely to increase student learning and student achievement.

Look back in your Participant Workbook at the Student Achievement activity that you completed following Session 1. Were there any learning and achievement gaps between various groups? Schools and districts implement a digital conversion with the key principle of increasing student learning and eliminating those gaps in student achievement.

Complete the Diversity Challenge activity in your Participant Workbook before continuing. When you are ready, click Next to continue.

Before continuing, please respond to the Session 2 Pause and Reflect questions in the Participant Workbook.

When you are ready, click Next to continue.

In general, beliefs are hard to change. But it is extremely important for learning to have students surrounded by people who believe that all students can learn and achieve at high levels.

Actions have been shown to change people’s beliefs and expectations. This can have a profound effect in schools and classrooms. If a classroom, school, or district purposefully and strategically pursues a diversity of approaches, techniques, and strategies, and the educators and administrations find the changes to be successful, then their beliefs and expectations about what students can accomplish are then raised. This, in turn, influences other practices and encourages further changes, and the cycle continues.

In order for members of the district to have an impact on student learning, everyone must believe that every child can learn and think at a high level. Digital conversion is about exploring a diversity of approaches, techniques, and strategies with the intent of increasing student achievement and influencing beliefs and expectations about students and their learning.

It’s not enough that educators, administrators, and parents believe that all children can learn. The students must also believe that they can learn and achieve at high levels. One way of encouraging this belief in students is to ensure that the way you speak to and interact with students implies that intelligence is more about hard work and less about genetics.

Dr. Carol S. Dweck explores the concept of fixed and growth mindsets in her book Mindset: The New Psychology of Success. People who have fixed mindsets believe that intelligence is fixed and that there is very little people can do to change their intelligence. People with growth mindsets believe that you need to work hard to become smart. In general, having a growth mindset leads to success. Teachers and other adults that students interact with need to have a growth mindset for their students in order to realize the moral imperative of digital conversion.

Listen to the podcast interview with Dr. Dweck in which she explains how to help children develop a growth mindset. As you listen, answer the following questions in your Participant Workbook:

·What is the relationship between growth mindsets and a digital conversion initiative?

·In what ways can you support a growth mindset for your students?

You just heard from Dr. Carol S. Dweck about praising students’ efforts rather than their smarts. Now, let’s take a quick look at an excerpt from the book Every Child, Every Day: A Digital Conversion Model for Student Achievement. In this excerpt, you will read about specific examples of how the digital conversion initiative at Mooresville Graded School District-along with high expectations for students-allowed special education students, English language learners, and minorities to make substantial progress.

Read pages 19 through 21 in Every Child, Every Day: A Digital Conversion Model for Student Achievement. While you read, use the T-chart in your Participant Workbook to provide specific passages from the text and to make notes about those passages and how digital tools and high expectations worked together to ensure students’ success.

Think about the information that you’ve learned from the course so far, especially the information that you’ve learned about moral imperative, beliefs and expectations, creating a growth mindset, and how digital tools and high expectations build students’ success.

Review your responses to the Diversity Challenge activity that you completed earlier in this session. Think about the types of students that you identified as being hard to teach. Respond to the following questions in your Participant Workbook:

·How can digital tools help you meet the needs of your challenging students in the Diversity Challenge activity?

·How might digital conversion change your expectations for what your students can accomplish or achieve?

Now, you’ll have a chance to watch part of an Investigations for the Common Core lesson and observe how an Investigations teacher implements some of the Investigations lesson features that you just learned about. After watching the video, you will be asked to respond to two reflection questions in your Participant Workbook.

Write down three or four points from the video that resonated with you. Think about how you can use each point in your own work. For example, you may have had a similar experience as the teacher, Heather Graham, in which you have limited books available for students to read at their levels and on a particular topic. You may want to note how you have the same limitations and how you can use technology as she did to create additional opportunities for students to read and learn.



When you are ready, click Next to continue.

Increasing student achievement and preparing students for their futures-whether they pursue college or go straight into a career-is a moral imperative that the whole school community must share. When people understand the potential outcomes of a digital conversion, they are likely to encourage others and find ways to support the changes that take place. Watch an interview with Dr. Mark Edwards to hear him discuss the moral imperative and high expectations that the community had for their students and the digital conversion. Click Play to watch the video. Click Next to continue.

Respond to the following question in your Participant Workbook:

How will you convey your moral imperative and high expectations to others?


When you are ready, click Next to continue.

It’s time to share your thoughts with your peers! Go to the Discussion Board, and respond to the Session 2 Discussion Board questions as you reflect on the moral imperative that supports a digital conversion. When you are ready, click Next to continue.

Let’s review the objectives for this session.

·Understand the definition of moral imperative.

·Explain the relationship between high expectations and the moral imperative for digital conversion.


Now, let’s review what you have learned in this session.

You began by looking at a definition of moral imperative, explored your own moral imperative for your role in the school or district, and looked at the moral imperative behind digital conversion.

Then, you learned about the role of beliefs and expectations in learning. You listened to a podcast interview on creating a growth mindset in children and then reflected on how digital conversion can help meet the needs of a variety of students.

Next, you watched a video on the impact of digital conversion on student achievement in which a teacher and a principal shared how digital conversion has had an impact in the classroom.

Finally, you watched a video in which Dr. Edwards described the effects of having a community that supported the moral imperative behind a digital conversion.

In the next session, you’ll learn about the need for a culture of caring and how to create such a culture in your classroom, school, or district.

Be sure to complete the following tasks before beginning self-paced Session 3:

·Read Chapter 3, Chapter 4, and pages 149 through 159 of Every Child, Every Day: A Digital Conversion Model for Student Achievement.

·Apply the knowledge gained from this session to your role in the school or district before completing the next session. Record your experience in your Participant Workbook.

·Answer Discussion Board questions, and respond to two other participants’ posts.

Now, show what you know! Visit the course homepage to take the assessment for Session 2.

We’ll see you again in Session 3!
